title: GitOps & Observability Platform
summary: A multi-node KIND cluster that reconciles itself from git: Go microservice with Prometheus RED metrics in a minimal non-root image, parameterised Helm chart with ServiceMonitor and an optional HPA, GitHub Actions gating on kubeconform, Helm lint and GHCR publishing, Argo CD with self-healing, and Grafana fed by kube-prometheus-stack plus Loki/Promtail.

chapters.title: Architecture and traffic flow
paragraphs: Three paths run through this cluster and they meet in one place. A request arrives from a browser and ends at a pod. A scrape arrives from Prometheus and ends at the same pod, on a different port path. And a `git push` ends at the cluster itself, rewriting what those pods are running. Everything below is what the manifests in the repository actually declare.

The first thing worth saying is what is *not* here. There is no cloud load balancer, because KIND has none to offer — the cluster is three Docker containers on one machine. `kind-config.yaml` binds host port 80 straight into the control-plane container and labels that node `ingress-ready=true`, which is the hook the NGINX ingress controller is scheduled against. That single line is what makes `localhost` resolve to a real ingress rather than to nothing.

The second is the boundary between the three. The application, its chart and the wiring all live in this repository. The stack the wiring assumes — the Prometheus Operator, Grafana and its sidecar, Loki and Promtail — is installed alongside it as separate Helm releases. That is why the chart renders a `ServiceMonitor` it cannot itself satisfy: the resource is a contract with an operator that has to already be there.
chapters.tradeoff: Every box and arrow above is one machine. The ingress path works because a Docker port binding happens to land on the node the controller was scheduled to, and that is a property of this laptop rather than of the design. Nothing here has been tested against a second node failing, a real load balancer, or a network that can partition — so the diagram is an accurate map of what runs, and not evidence that the shape survives anywhere else.

topology.note: Between 03 and 04 sits the Service, which is not inside any node — it is a cluster-scoped ClusterIP that gives the two pods one stable address, taking :80 and forwarding to targetPort 8080. The Ingress rule is cluster-scoped too. Both are routing objects rather than things that run somewhere, which is why neither has a box.

chapters.title: Monitoring ships with the chart
paragraphs: The Helm chart does not stop at Deployment, Service, and Ingress. It also renders a `ServiceMonitor` so Prometheus discovers the target without anyone editing scrape config, plus a PodDisruptionBudget, a NetworkPolicy and a PrometheusRule. An HPA ships in the chart as well, parameterised but disabled by default — it is available, not active. The Grafana dashboard sits beside the chart rather than inside it, as a ConfigMap carrying the sidecar label, so it loads when the monitoring stack is installed.

The reason is that observability added later is observability that does not exist. If the scrape config is a separate step, it stays a separate step: the service ships, the ticket to add monitoring gets written, and it sits in the backlog until the first incident makes it urgent. Putting the `ServiceMonitor` and the alerting rules in the chart means the only way to deploy this service is to deploy it scraped.

The dashboard did not get the same treatment, and that is the honest gap. It lives in `kubernetes/grafana/` and is applied by hand, outside the Argo CD application, which points only at `helm/demo-app`. So a renamed metric updates the panel in the same commit but not in the same deploy. Half the argument is implemented; the other half is still a manifest I remember to apply.
chapters.tradeoff: Chart complexity. The chart is larger than the workload strictly requires and carries a hard assumption that the Prometheus Operator's CRDs are already installed — without them `helm install` fails outright on unknown kinds rather than degrading quietly. I took a chart that is harder to reuse over a service that can be deployed unobserved. The dashboard sitting outside it is the part I have not finished.

chapters.title: Trivy gating
paragraphs: Trivy runs against the built image before it is pushed, and the job fails on CRITICAL. Failing means the image never reaches the registry, so a vulnerable tag is never something ArgoCD could pull even by accident.

The severity line is where the judgement is. Gating on everything, MEDIUM and LOW included, produces a pipeline that is red most mornings for findings nobody is going to act on, and a red pipeline that is normal is the same as no pipeline. Gating on CRITICAL alone keeps a failure worth reading — but the same setting also filters the report, so HIGH findings are not shown at all rather than shown and ignored. That is a narrower net than I would want on a service carrying real traffic, and it is worth being precise that the gate hides them rather than merely tolerating them.

There is a second, quieter decision: unfixed vulnerabilities are ignored. A CRITICAL with no patched version available is not something a build can fix, and blocking on it means blocking every deploy until an upstream maintainer acts. But `--ignore-unfixed` drops them from the report rather than merely letting them through, so they are not visible in the output either. The gate blocks what a rebuild can fix and stays silent about the rest — and the silence is the part worth knowing about.
chapters.tradeoff: Ignoring unfixed findings is a real hole — a critical vulnerability with no patch is still a critical vulnerability, and my pipeline will happily ship it. I accepted that because the alternative is a gate that gets disabled the first week it blocks something urgent, and a gate that is switched off protects nothing at all.

chapters.title: Verifying self-healing
paragraphs: Self-healing is the claim that is easiest to make and least often checked. `selfHeal: true` is one line of YAML in the ArgoCD Application, and having written that line is not evidence that anything heals — it is evidence that you have read the documentation. The failure it guards against is not dramatic either. It is someone fixing something by hand at two in the morning, and that fix quietly becoming the real state of the cluster, diverging from the repository until a later deploy reverts it and nobody understands why.

So the test is deliberately crude, and deliberately run against the live cluster rather than a copy of it. Scale the deployment by hand — `kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=5` — which is exactly the kind of change a person makes under pressure and forgets to write down. Then watch two things at once: `kubectl get pods -w` in one pane, and the application in the ArgoCD interface in the other. The new pods start. Within seconds the application flips from Synced to OutOfSync, because ArgoCD watches cluster state rather than waiting on a polling interval. Then, with no pull request and nobody clicking Sync, the replica count returns to the number in `values.yaml` and the extra pods terminate.

What makes that convincing is the part that does not happen. There is no approval, no pipeline run, no human in the loop — the controller compares live state against Git, finds them different, and makes them the same. The manual change never survives long enough to become the truth. That is the entire argument for GitOps reduced to one observable event: the repository *is* the state of the cluster, not a description of what somebody once intended it to be.
chapters.tradeoff: The drift test proves reconciliation works for a change ArgoCD can see, in a field it manages, on a resource it owns. It proves nothing about drift in resources outside the application's scope, about a change applied and reverted between two reconciles, or about anything a controller cannot express as a diff against a manifest — a secret mutated after a pod has already read it, a change made at the node level, an admission webhook rewriting the object on the way in. It is a real test of the mechanism, and only of the mechanism.

differently.title: What I'd do differently
items: Split the deployment configuration into its own repository. CI commits the new image tag back into the same repository that triggered it, and the only thing stopping an infinite build loop is `[skip ci]` in the commit message. That is a convention holding back a structural problem — two repositories make the loop impossible rather than merely discouraged.

Sign the images and verify the signature at admission. Right now the cluster trusts any tag that reaches GHCR under the right name. Cosign plus a policy controller would close the gap between 'my pipeline built this' and 'the cluster will run this'.

Put the Helm chart under test. It is rendered and validated with kubeconform and helm lint, but never asserted on — there is no check that the ServiceMonitor selector still matches the Service labels after a refactor. That is the kind of break that shows up as a silently missing dashboard weeks later.

Write down why the Trivy gate stops at CRITICAL. Gating on CRITICAL and ignoring unfixed findings were both deliberate, and both are defensible on a cluster nobody depends on. I never recorded the point at which that stops being true, which means nobody — including me — knows when to tighten it.
